title: Crypto Infrastructure Hub
subtitle: Trace organizations, legal records, assets, networks, cash legs and operating clocks end to end
evidence_cutoff: 2026-10-03 XRP Asia and APAC Ripple entity refresh; 2026-09-30 CSD BR and Ripple record-mirror refresh; 2026-09-27 technology buildout, specialist-system and Quant value-capture refresh; 2026-09-26 Major bank transition comparison; 2026-09-24 Fed GENIUS proposal room; 2026-09-22 Transition Gates comparison; other sources retain their dates
thesis: Crypto infrastructure is a system of systems. The useful question is not only which chain carries a token, but which entity owes the claim, which record controls title, which operator can correct it, where the cash settles, and which parts are proposed, piloted or actually live.
boundary: Technical finality, authoritative legal record and cash or redemption remedy are separate endpoints. Proposal, staff position, registration, ownership, partnership, software capability, pilot and production are different facts and clocks.

process_roles.label: Controller
process_roles.description: Sets the binding rule, owns the authoritative record or liability, or has final decision rights at this stage.

process_roles.label: Operator
process_roles.description: Performs the stage's core regulated, financial, recordkeeping, clearing or settlement function.

process_roles.label: Integrator
process_roles.description: Connects systems, messages, routes, assets or participants without automatically controlling the claim or finality.

process_roles.label: External dependency
process_roles.description: Supplies a required institution, market, network, legal regime or service outside the focal ecosystem's control.

scale_states.label: Not applicable
scale_states.description: Scale is not a meaningful measure for this legal, control or dependency fact.

scale_states.label: Scale not public
scale_states.description: The capability or relationship is evidenced, but no authoritative public receipt establishes its operating scale.

scale_states.label: Single event
scale_states.description: Evidence establishes one transaction, demonstration, issuance or bounded operating event.

scale_states.label: Bounded cohort
scale_states.description: Operation is limited to named participants, instruments, corridors, networks or a pilot perimeter.

scale_states.label: Generally available
scale_states.description: The service or network is available to its eligible target population; availability does not prove route share or use.

scale_states.label: Reported aggregate
scale_states.description: The source reports an aggregate that combines activities and cannot be treated as this process stage's volume.

scale_states.label: Material process volume
scale_states.description: Authoritative evidence establishes sustained volume material to this exact process stage.

stress_states.label: Not applicable
stress_states.description: Stress evidence is not a meaningful measure for this legal, control or dependency fact.

stress_states.label: Stress evidence not public
stress_states.description: No authoritative public evidence establishes failure or recovery performance.

stress_states.label: No demonstrated stress test
stress_states.description: The system is described or operating, but reviewed sources do not establish a relevant controlled or observed stress outcome.

stress_states.label: Contractual controls only
stress_states.description: Terms allocate correction or failure authority, but no observed stress outcome proves the controls in use.

stress_states.label: Controlled test
stress_states.description: A tabletop, simulation, pilot or other bounded exercise tested failure or recovery behavior.

stress_states.label: Observed stress
stress_states.description: The process encountered a real disruption, run, default, outage or comparable stress with documented outcomes.

process_maps.label: Tokenization
process_maps.description: See which ecosystems define, issue, record, move, settle, service and repair a tokenized security or property claim.
process_maps.boundary: The token, underlying asset, authoritative ownership record, cash leg, clearing guarantee and legal remedy may sit in different systems. Network transfer never supplies the missing layers by implication.

stages.label: Claim & authority
stages.description: Define the asset, issuer, holder rights, governing law and operative permissions.
stages.question: What does the token legally represent, who owes the claim and which authority governs it?

stages.label: Admission & identity
stages.description: Admit the issuer, instrument, participant, custodian, wallet, venue and network.
stages.question: Who and what may enter the process, and is admission approved, enabled or only proposed?

stages.label: Underlying & collateral
stages.description: Deposit, immobilize, lock, custody or otherwise control the underlying position and collateral.
stages.question: Where is the underlying asset held, who controls it and what prevents duplicate issuance?

stages.label: Instruction & issuance
stages.description: Authenticate and execute issuance, trade, transfer, tokenization or detokenization instructions.
stages.question: Which event creates the binding transaction and which system mints, burns or transfers the token?

stages.label: Authoritative record
stages.description: Update the controlling registered-owner, transfer-agent, depository, issuer or entitlement record.
stages.question: If chain, issuer, transfer-agent, depository and customer books disagree, which record controls?

stages.label: Custody, access & market
stages.description: Provide investor access, custody, distribution, venue, matching and trading functions.
stages.question: Who can hold or trade, through which regulated entity and under what product-specific restrictions?

stages.label: Transport & interoperability
stages.description: Move or synchronize token state and messages across networks and linked systems.
stages.question: Which rail transports the representation, and which legal and recovery functions remain external?

stages.label: Liquidity & collateral
stages.description: Identify funding and collateral availability for the transaction.
stages.question: Who supplies liquidity or collateral, and on what terms?

stages.label: Clearing
stages.description: Identify matching, netting or guarantee of obligations.
stages.question: Who calculates, nets or guarantees the obligation?

stages.label: Cash-leg delivery
stages.description: Identify delivery of the cash-leg asset, which may itself be an issuer claim rather than final bank cash discharge.
stages.question: What cash-leg asset is delivered, and which issuer or bank still owes a claim afterward?

stages.label: Cash redemption & payout
stages.description: Identify redemption of a cash claim or payout through the bank settlement system; distinguish the obligation from evidence of completed payout.
stages.question: Who redeems or pays out the claim, through which system, and is completion established?

stages.label: Legal finality
stages.description: Identify when rights transfer or obligations are legally discharged.
stages.question: What establishes legal title or final discharge, beyond technical completion?

stages.label: Posting & servicing
stages.description: Reconcile books and administer continuing holder rights.
stages.question: Who posts the record and administers distributions, votes or redemption?

stages.label: Remedy, default & proof
stages.description: Repair errors, allocate default losses, test available support and state what production evidence actually proves.
stages.question: Who can reverse, claw back or correct, who bears loss and what scale or stress evidence exists?

process_maps.label: Stablecoins
process_maps.description: See which ecosystems issue, reserve, distribute, transport, redeem and support a stablecoin claim.
process_maps.boundary: Issuer liability, reserve custody, token supply, distribution, chain transport, liquidity, bank payout and any public backstop remain separate legal and operating layers.

stages.label: Issuer & authority
stages.description: Identify the exact token, issuer, redemption obligor, holder claim and governing perimeter.
stages.question: Who owes redemption and which effective authority permits the exact issuer?

stages.label: Admission & eligibility
stages.description: Establish eligibility for issuers, distributors, reserve custodians, wallets, networks and redemption customers.
stages.question: Who may issue, distribute, hold, transport and redeem directly?

stages.label: Reserves & custody
stages.description: Fund and custody eligible reserves with exact ownership, segregation, valuation and liquidity treatment.
stages.question: Where are reserves held, whose property are they and what happens if issuer or custodian fails?

stages.label: Mint & burn
stages.description: Authenticate mint, freeze, burn, reissue and redemption instructions and update token state.
stages.question: What authorizes supply change, and must incoming or outgoing cash already be final?

stages.label: Liability record
stages.description: Reconcile the issuer's liability, supply, reserve, custodian, distributor and customer records.
stages.question: Which record proves outstanding liability and how is it reconciled to supply and reserves?

stages.label: Access, custody & distribution
stages.description: Provide customer access, custody, wallet, exchange and distribution channels.
stages.question: Which exact entity holds, distributes or services the token, and what rights do indirect holders have?

stages.label: Network transport
stages.description: Transfer or bridge supported token representations across named networks.
stages.question: Which network or bridge moves the token and who controls recovery when records diverge?

stages.label: Liquidity & conversion
stages.description: Supply token inventory, quotes and supported conversion routes between assets.
stages.question: Who supplies liquidity or converts the token, and what depth or usage is evidenced?

stages.label: Clearing
stages.description: Match or net obligations and identify any novation or guarantee separately from exchange execution.
stages.question: Who matches, nets, novates or guarantees the obligations, under which rules?

stages.label: Cash payout
stages.description: Perform the actual fiat or wholesale-money payment and account posting outside token transfer.
stages.question: Who pays which money to which account, and what confirms the cash posting?

stages.label: Issuer redemption
stages.description: Accept eligible redemption requests and retire the issuer claim under applicable terms.
stages.question: Who owes redemption, who may request it, and which conditions govern acceptance?

stages.label: Legal discharge
stages.description: Identify the rule and event that finally discharge the obligation; separate this from token confirmation and cash availability.
stages.question: Under which rule is the obligation irrevocably discharged, and can a court or insolvency process unwind it?

stages.label: Remedy, stress & proof
stages.description: Govern freezes, mistakes, bridge failures, depegs, runs, insolvency, loss allocation and any public response.
stages.question: Who can repair or freeze, who bears a shortfall and what circulation, redemption or stress evidence exists?

coverage.summary: OUSD token confirmation, accepted Bridge redemption, bank payout and discharge of an underlying commercial obligation are separate legal events.
coverage.boundary: No universal OUSD finality rule makes every chain transfer a final Mastercard payment, bank credit or irreversible legal discharge across jurisdictions and insolvency processes.

process_maps.label: FX & cross-border
process_maps.description: See which ecosystems quote, fund, route, convert, clear and finally settle a cross-border payment.
process_maps.boundary: Customer credit, a message, a token movement and a shared-ledger commitment are not automatically final interbank settlement. Each currency claim, inventory owner, cash leg and remedy must be named.

stages.label: Claims & authority
stages.description: Define both currency claims, debtors, purpose, jurisdictions, governing rules and any bridge asset.
stages.question: What exact claims are exchanged, who owes each one and which corridor rules apply?

stages.label: Parties & corridor
stages.description: Admit customers, banks, correspondents, dealers, wallets, networks and accounts under KYC, sanctions and capital controls.
stages.question: Which parties and systems may legally participate in this corridor?

stages.label: Funding & inventory
stages.description: Prefund accounts, secure credit, post collateral or acquire and finance currency or bridge inventory.
stages.question: Who supplies each asset, where is it held and is liquidity prefunded or credit-dependent?

stages.label: Mandate & quote
stages.description: Authenticate payment instructions, beneficiary details, quote, rate window and settlement instructions.
stages.question: Who selected the rate and route, under what mandate and for how long is the quote binding?

stages.label: Execution & route
stages.description: Form the FX and payment obligations with exact counterparties, price, spread, venue and selected route.
stages.question: Which entities became bound and who assumed market, inventory and replacement-cost risk?

stages.label: Messaging & transport
stages.description: Record messages, funded commitments, token movements and shared-ledger or interoperability events.
stages.question: Which event communicates or transports the payment, and which required institutions remain outside that rail?

stages.label: Clearing & PvP
stages.description: Match, net, novate, guarantee or synchronize the currency legs through an actual clearing or PvP mechanism.
stages.question: Who clears or guarantees the legs, and is principal risk truly eliminated?

stages.label: Authoritative records
stages.description: Identify the legally authoritative deposit, account, token-holder or securityholder books and who may update them.
stages.question: Which record controls the claim, and who has authority to correct it?

stages.label: Cash transfer
stages.description: Move the actual cash claim through banks, issuer redemption arrangements or a named settlement system.
stages.question: Which money claim moves, through whose account, and which external institutions remain necessary?

stages.label: Legal finality
stages.description: Identify the rule and event that discharge each payment or currency obligation.
stages.question: When is each leg legally final, under which terms, and is that conclusion publicly established?

stages.label: Customer payout / posting
stages.description: Deliver cash or credit to the customer and reconcile the customer-facing account.
stages.question: What did the beneficiary receive, when was it available, and was credit provisional?

stages.label: Returns, default & proof
stages.description: Handle rejects, recalls, sanctions holds, fraud, failed legs, defaults, loss allocation and any official support.
stages.question: Who repairs or returns a payment, who bears loss and what route, volume, liquidity or stress evidence exists?

ecosystems.label: Ripple / XRPL
ecosystems.description: Follow Ripple from the operating company through acquired product lines, exact regulated entities, RLUSD and XRP, XRPL transport, market access and the SEC proposal overlap.
ecosystems.boundary: Ripple, its subsidiaries and products, XRPL, XRP and RLUSD are separate legal and technical objects; an edge records a reviewed relationship, not a merger of roles.
walkthrough: Steering: Ripple is the company parent; XRPL is a public network rather than a Ripple-owned subsidiary.
Operating stack: Payments, custody, prime brokerage, treasury and wallet services sit in distinct product and acquired-company branches.
Charter clock: Ripple National Trust Bank has preliminary conditional OCC approval but is not yet an operating national trust bank.
Asset control: Standard Custody is the named U.S. RLUSD issuer; XRP is XRPL's native asset, not Ripple equity or RLUSD backing.

Treasury and lending: Evernorth and Pathfinder are separate legal entities from Ripple; pre-close XRP remains under exact custody and escrow restrictions, while Evernorth's Single Asset Vault and XLS-66 participation remains proposed.
Execution: XRPL provides ledger, DEX and pathfinding functions; Wormhole and the XRPL EVM sidechain extend transport and application reach.

Cash and access: BNY holds the reviewed RLUSD reserve-custody and transaction-banking roles; Ripple Prime is separately an early adopter of BNY's private-platform tokenized deposits; exact Hidden Road entities hold reviewed DTC and FICC access.
Legal endpoint: Customer, issuer, custodian, transfer-agent and market-utility records remain decisive for title, redemption and settlement.
Policy overlap: Ripple's SEC submission is advocacy; proposal-fit edges show architectural touchpoints, not SEC adoption or approval.

ecosystems.label: Securitize
ecosystems.description: Follow the public parent through separately regulated subsidiaries, fund products, their transfer-agent record, chain representations and cash-leg connections.
ecosystems.boundary: The public parent, transfer agent, broker-dealer/ATS, adviser, administrator, fund sponsor, fund shares and networks remain distinct.
walkthrough: Steering: Securitize Corp. is the public parent, while permissions attach to named subsidiaries.
Operating roles: Transfer agency, brokerage/ATS, investment advice and fund administration are separate regulated or operating functions.
Asset layer: BUIDL and VBILL are fund shares sponsored by their managers, not native chain assets.
Record layer: The transfer-agent control book remains distinct from wallet and chain position records.
Transport: Wormhole and named networks carry supported representations and movements.
Cash leg: Eligible product functions can exchange supported shares to RLUSD without making RLUSD the fund register.
Legal endpoint: The issuer, governing documents, transfer agent and regulated intermediaries determine rights and remedies.

ecosystems.label: Ethereum
ecosystems.description: Follow Ethereum governance, client software, validators, execution, applications, ETH economics, scaling layers and external asset authorities.
ecosystems.boundary: Ethereum provides execution and consensus; token issuers, application operators, custodians and legal recordkeepers retain their own authority.
walkthrough: Steering: Protocol change emerges through an open governance process; the Ethereum Foundation is influential but not a network owner.
Operation: Independent client teams and validators implement and secure the network.
Execution: EVM smart contracts create application logic and token interfaces.
Native asset: ETH pays adaptive fees, is burned under the fee mechanism and can be staked for consensus.
Scaling and transport: Layer-2 systems and bridges extend execution but add their own operators and control surfaces.
Asset authority: Issuers and applications control contract permissions and off-chain rights for their assets.
Legal endpoint: Ethereum finality does not by itself determine the legally authoritative holder record or remedy.

ecosystems.label: Hedera
ecosystems.description: Follow Hedera from Governing Council and open-source code through network services, HBAR, enterprise deployment and tokenized-asset operators.
ecosystems.boundary: Council governance, node operation, application control and legal-asset authority are separate layers.
walkthrough: Steering: The Hedera Governing Council sets network policy and governance.
Code: Hiero houses the reviewed open-source codebase and developer project.
Operation: Consensus nodes run the public mainnet and expose native services.
Native asset: HBAR pays fees and supports network security; it is not an enterprise tokenized asset.
Applications: HashSphere and other enterprise surfaces use Hedera services for controlled deployments.
Asset authority: Archax and other issuers or operators retain responsibility for the instruments they issue or service.
Legal endpoint: Network consensus does not replace issuer, custodian or regulated-record obligations.

ecosystems.label: Stellar
ecosystems.description: Follow Stellar from foundation and protocol governance through validators, anchors, Soroban applications, XLM, token issuers and institutional deployments.
ecosystems.boundary: The Stellar ledger, anchors, issuers, applications and regulated product records are separate authorities.
walkthrough: Steering: The Stellar Development Foundation supports protocol development and ecosystem growth without owning every node or asset.
Operation: Independent validators reach agreement under the Stellar Consensus Protocol.
Execution: The ledger supports native asset operations while Soroban adds smart-contract applications.
Native asset: XLM pays network fees and supports account reserves; it is not every issued asset's backing.
Access: Anchors and money-service integrations connect fiat and ledger assets.
Institutional products: BENJI and the reviewed DTC initiative retain their own legal, issuer and recordkeeping layers.
Legal endpoint: Issuer and regulated records control redemption, title and remedies beyond ledger settlement.

ecosystems.label: Canton
ecosystems.description: Follow Canton from protocol steward and application provider through participant validators, the Global Synchronizer, Canton Coin and named capital-markets applications.
ecosystems.boundary: Canton connects synchronized applications while preserving separate operators, data domains and legal books and records.
walkthrough: Steering: The Canton Foundation governs shared-network matters; application providers and participants keep separate authority.
Software and applications: Digital Asset develops core technology and operates products, but it is not every application or participant.
Operation: Participant validators process private workflows and connect through the Global Synchronizer.
Native utility: Canton Coin supplies network incentives and fees; it is not the securities or cash represented in applications.
Market applications: Broadridge, Tradeweb and DTC initiatives connect their own institutional workflows; one Tradeweb Treasury-for-USDCx transaction is completed but remains a single-event receipt.
Privacy and interoperability: synchronization coordinates authorized events without creating one universal data owner.
Legal endpoint: Each connected market and regulated entity retains its own settlement, record and remedy rules.

ecosystems.label: Solana
ecosystems.description: Follow Solana governance and validators through runtime, token programs, SOL economics, issuer applications and institutional tokenization.
ecosystems.boundary: Solana execution, token-program controls and issuer or regulated records are separate sources of authority.
walkthrough: Steering: The Solana Foundation supports decentralization and ecosystem work without owning every validator or application.
Operation: Validators execute transactions and reach network consensus.
Execution: Programs and accounts supply the application runtime.
Token controls: Token-2022 and related programs expose issuer-selected controls.
Native asset: SOL pays base and priority fees and supports staking.
Applications and transport: Issuers, BUIDL and Wormhole use the network while retaining their own operational roles.
Legal endpoint: Chain confirmation does not alone determine legal title, redemption or regulated recordkeeping.

ecosystems.label: Avalanche
ecosystems.description: Follow Avalanche governance and software through the Primary Network, validators, AVAX, custom L1s and permissioned institutional deployments.
ecosystems.boundary: The Primary Network, custom Avalanche L1s, their validator policies and application legal records must be evaluated separately.
walkthrough: Steering: The Avalanche Foundation and Ava Labs support different governance, development and ecosystem roles.
Operation: Validators secure the Primary Network under its staking rules.
Native asset: AVAX pays fees and supports staking on the Primary Network.
Custom networks: Avalanche L1s can define their own validator and permission structures.
Institutional deployments: Evergreen provides patterns for controlled financial applications.
Product use: BUIDL availability is a product deployment, not Avalanche ownership of the fund.
Legal endpoint: Each L1 and application retains its own operators, asset authorities and legal settlement rules.

ecosystems.label: Chainlink
ecosystems.description: Follow Chainlink Labs, decentralized oracle networks, data feeds, CCIP, CRE, LINK economics and financial-market infrastructure integrations.
ecosystems.boundary: Chainlink supplies middleware and coordination; it does not become the issuer, custodian, transfer agent or settlement authority for connected assets.
walkthrough: Steering: Chainlink Labs develops and supports products; decentralized oracle networks execute services.
Operation: Independent node operators aggregate data and perform jobs.
Data layer: Feeds bring external observations into on-chain applications.
Transport: CCIP passes verified messages and token instructions across supported environments.
Execution: CRE coordinates multi-system workflows around data, identity and settlement steps.
Native asset: LINK is used in service economics and staking, not as the legal asset being transferred.
Legal endpoint: Connected institutions and ledgers retain asset, record, custody and settlement authority.

ecosystems.label: Bitcoin
ecosystems.description: Follow Bitcoin from open-source rules and node validation through miners, transactions, BTC fee economics, Lightning and institutional custody wrappers.
ecosystems.boundary: Bitcoin consensus validates network transactions; custodians, exchanges, funds and payment providers add separate ownership and legal-record layers.
walkthrough: Steering: Bitcoin Core is open-source software; rule adoption depends on users and node operators rather than a company owner.
Validation: Full nodes enforce the rules they run and independently verify transactions and blocks.
Ordering: Miners assemble candidate blocks and compete to extend the chain.
Native asset: BTC is the network asset and transaction fees compensate block inclusion.
Second layer: Lightning adds payment channels and routing above the base chain.
Access and wrappers: Custodians, exchanges and ETPs create separate account and beneficial-ownership records.
Legal endpoint: Base-chain possession and an intermediary claim are different forms of control and remedy.

ecosystems.label: DTC / DTCC tokenization
ecosystems.description: Follow DTC from conditional SEC staff posture through the issuer register, participant entitlement, token conversion, official DTC record, correction controls and operating clocks.
ecosystems.boundary: Cede, the participant entitlement, LedgerScan and the chain token are related but distinct records.
walkthrough: Start with the conditional SEC staff position, not a final rule or approval.
Separate DTCC parent, DTC regulated operator and DTCC Digital software roles.
Keep Cede as issuer-register holder and the participant account as the conventional entitlement.
Move the underlying into DTC’s Digital Omnibus Account before Factory minting.
Transfer only among registered wallets while LedgerScan maintains DTC’s official token record.
Preserve DTC root controls, detokenization and corporate-action correction paths.
End with July limited production, expected October launch and planned Stellar availability.

ecosystems.label: Cash legs & tokenized bank money
ecosystems.description: Compare stablecoins, commercial-bank deposit tokens, central-bank-backed settlement units and orchestration layers without treating them as interchangeable cash.
ecosystems.boundary: Issuer liability, representation, orchestration and legal discharge remain separate.
walkthrough: Identify the money issuer: central bank, commercial bank or stablecoin issuer.
Identify the legal claim: reserve, deposit, redemption right or payment-system balance.
Identify its representation: conventional account, private ledger or public-chain token.
Identify eligible access: customer, vetted wallet, participant or settlement bank.
Identify the orchestration layer: application, Swift, Partior or smart contract.
Locate final settlement or redemption on bank books, RTGS, reserve pool or same ledger.
Preserve correction, insolvency, downtime and operating-clock boundaries.

ecosystems.label: Circle / USDC / CPN / Arc / Tazapay
ecosystems.kind: dual issuer + stablecoin + payment network + L1 + pending acquisition
ecosystems.description: Trace Circle from exact issuers and institutional mint access through reserves, native USDC, CPN orchestration, Tazapay's live fiat endpoints, cross-chain transport, Arc’s private-mainnet clock and the separately pending Tazapay acquisition.
ecosystems.boundary: Circle parent, issuer, reserve pool, software services, CPN operator, Tazapay legal entities and licences, acquisition purchaser, Arc operator and validators are distinct objects; the Tazapay agreement has not closed.
walkthrough: Identify the public parent without treating it as the issuer.
Trace Coinbase's minority stake, USDC distribution role and reserve-income economics without treating Coinbase as issuer or reserve obligor.
Choose the exact USDC issuer by holder jurisdiction.
Enter through Circle Mint only if institutionally eligible.
Trace dollar funding into issuer-specific segregated reserves.
Mint USDC with its conditional redemption right and administrative controls.
Separate Circle Technology Services' CPN orchestration from the participating institutions that hold, convert and pay funds.
Follow Tazapay's already-live CPN partnership from stablecoin receipt and conversion to local bank payout, preserving the exact licensed-entity boundary.
Keep Taurus's signed acquisition agreement on the announced clock until regulatory approvals and closing establish control.
Compare native CCTP burn/mint with Gateway’s unified balance.
End at Arc public mainnet, then separate current launch operation from future proof-of-stake, privacy, scaling and ARC-token roadmap items.

ecosystems.label: Coinbase / Base / Tokenize
ecosystems.description: Follow Coinbase from its public parent through the exact ADGM issuer, OML title record, underlying share custody, B20 representation, Base execution and Ethereum finality.
ecosystems.boundary: Wallet possession, Base state, OML Legal Register and underlying share custody are separate records.
walkthrough: Establish the Coinbase corporate chain.
Separate Coinbase's USDC distribution and reserve-income economics from Circle's issuer governance and redemption duties.
Separate certificate issuer, tokenisation/CSD operator and underlying broker-custodian.
Apply the primary-market eligibility and current in-kind creation rules.
Place the share in the segregated underlying-property account.
Mint the B20 certificate on Base and pay ETH gas.
Pass secondary holders through vesting and sanctions eligibility.
End at OML’s Legal Register, intervention controls and redemption/burn process.

ecosystems.label: Algorand
ecosystems.description: Trace the public network, ALGO economics, post-quantum account capability, legal issuer objects and native USDC cash leg.
ecosystems.boundary: Falcon account authorization is live, but it does not make the entire consensus stack post-quantum or turn Algorand state into issuer title.
walkthrough: Start with the Foundation’s current stewardship role.
Pass through independent validators and public-network finality.
Separate ALGO fee/stake economics from issued assets.
Use Falcon accounts as an account-authorization overlay, not a whole-stack PQ label.
Identify Midas as legal product operator.
Represent mTBILL through the ASA primitive and exchange it against native USDC.
End at Algorand finality plus Midas and Circle redemption remedies.

ecosystems.label: XDC
ecosystems.description: Trace XDC from foundation and KYC masternodes through trade-document workflow and a pilot stablecoin cash leg.
ecosystems.boundary: A digital trade document or token needs a named bank undertaking, issuer, governing law and remedy beyond chain finality.
walkthrough: Separate Foundation provenance from the network.
Pass through KYC masternodes and XDPoS finality.
Keep XDC gas and stake economics separate from trade claims.
Identify the bank or authority behind the LC or trade document.
Use Contour as the workflow layer.
Treat Stable-Coin Lab and its USDC path as a pilot.
End at XDC finality plus bank, Circle and trade-law remedies.

ecosystems.label: IOTA / TWIN
ecosystems.description: Trace IOTA from protocol and TWIN governance through validators, TLIP trade-document exchange, named authorities and the still-developing payment layer.
ecosystems.boundary: IOTA proofs and TLIP exchange do not replace customs, identity or legal-record issuers.
walkthrough: Separate IOTA Foundation from TWIN’s multistakeholder governance.
Pass through public validators and Starfish technical finality.
Keep IOTA token economics separate from trade-document rights.
Locate the exact customs, identity or document issuer.
Exchange records through TLIP without moving source authority.
Treat ADAPT country implementations as pilots and the payment layer as planned.
End at chain finality plus agency, customs and legal correction.

ecosystems.label: Wormhole
ecosystems.description: Trace Wormhole as a transport and messaging layer across named Securitize, XRPL and RLUSD connections without promoting it into the issuer, title record, custodian or cash rail.
ecosystems.boundary: Cross-chain transport does not itself preserve legal title, supply cash, discharge an obligation or determine the remedy when source, destination and authoritative records disagree.
walkthrough: Start with Wormhole as the interoperability provider.
Identify the source chain, destination chain and supported asset representation.
Separate message verification and transfer mechanics from issuer control.
Locate the transfer agent, legal register or other authoritative record outside the bridge.
Locate the reserve, custodian and cash leg outside the bridge.
Keep each named integration on its own operating clock.
End at the external correction, recovery and legal-remedy authority.

ecosystems.label: Quant (bounded)
ecosystems.kind: proprietary orchestration + live customer pilot + planned U.S. network
ecosystems.description: Bounded profile for Quant’s proprietary interoperability products, Fusion platform, first GBTD live customer transactions, The Clearing House selection and Murex capability.
ecosystems.boundary: Live customer cases and a supplier selection do not prove scaled bank production, authoritative-ledger control, general U.S. availability or QNT value capture.
walkthrough: Identify Quant Network Limited as the software provider.
Pass through Overledger and Flow as proprietary services.
Keep QNT economics separate from bank money.
Treat Fusion as a live platform with unresolved institutional operator detail.
Locate each participating bank’s own authoritative deposit record.
Keep GBTD's first live customer cases separate from a standing production service.
Keep The Clearing House selection separate from its expected H1 2027 availability and any QNT demand claim.
Keep Murex as production-ready capability rather than a named client deployment.
End at bank-book settlement and depositor remedy, with Rosalind historical only.

ecosystems.label: SWIFT ledger & bank obligations
ecosystems.description: 17 announced banks, six reported payment pairings across eight banks, and separately sourced adjacent projects. Open SWIFT banks & tests for the research and select a named payment trace.
ecosystems.boundary: Controlled live pilots; no required public coin established. Bank claims, coordination, cash discharge and legal finality are separate.
walkthrough: Evidence: 17 initial-use participants; six completed pairings across eight banks located through September 9. Nine banks have no completion receipt located.
Framework: published shared governance and regulated participation; executed participant terms remain unreviewed.
Operator: SWIFT runs coordination; participating banks retain money and settlement responsibility.
Issuer: participating banks retain deposit liabilities; SWIFT does not issue this money.
Funding: SWIFT describes upfront confirmation; the precise reservation or credit object remains undisclosed.
Coordination: SWIFT operates the shared commitment ledger on Besu/EVM software.
Clearing: UOB and HSBC report matched and netted obligations before external settlement.
Cash: FAB reports completed correspondent settlement outside the SWIFT ledger.
Customer clock: DBS reports a September 5 weekend USD payment in minutes; external-finality timing is not specified.
Failure: executed participant terms, loss allocation and stressed performance remain unresolved.

nodes.label: SEC proposal 34-106246
nodes.summary: Would modernize registered transfer-agent duties for electronic records, linked systems and DLT while preserving an accountable recordkeeping agent.
nodes.boundary: It does not approve Ripple, Securitize, Wormhole, XRPL, RLUSD, XRP or any chain.

nodes.label: Issuer-authorized security issue
nodes.summary: The issuer and governing corporate law define the security, authorized issuance and recognized holder rights before any technical representation is considered.
nodes.boundary: A token contract or wallet position does not independently create the issuer's legal obligation or displace governing law.

nodes.label: Registered recordkeeping transfer agent
nodes.summary: The proposal's accountable legal recordkeeper for a fungible issue, responsible for and in exclusive control of the master securityholder file even when multiple systems or service companies are used.
nodes.boundary: The Commission asks whether jointly responsible agents should be allowed as an alternative; the one-agent structure is not yet final.

nodes.label: Authoritative master securityholder file
nodes.summary: The proposed control book that identifies securityholders and positions across one or more electronic components, including possible blockchain or DLT records.
nodes.boundary: Not every ledger, token balance or transaction log is automatically the legally authoritative record.

nodes.label: Rule 17Ad-30 governance and outsourcing controls
nodes.summary: Written compliance procedures, annual governing-body approval and controlled use of service providers would keep outsourced technology inside the transfer agent's accountability environment.
nodes.boundary: Vendor use would not transfer the registered agent's legal responsibility to a chain, bridge or software provider.

nodes.label: Form TA-2 tokenization reporting
nodes.summary: The proposal would distinguish issuer-sponsored and third-party tokenization and report security type, DLT use and service providers.
nodes.boundary: Reporting a deployment would not constitute Commission approval of the asset, provider or network.

nodes.label: Rule 17Ad-31 legends and correction controls
nodes.summary: Restrictive legends, legal basis, red flags, safe-harbor conditions and correction/deletion duties would be made explicit, including questions about immutable records.
nodes.boundary: Append-only technical history and the legally corrected current state are not the same thing.

nodes.label: Securitize Corp.
nodes.summary: Public top parent after the July 2026 business combination; consolidated group includes separately regulated operating entities.
nodes.boundary: Top-parent control does not erase which subsidiary holds each registration, contract or customer duty.

nodes.label: Ripple Labs / Ripple
nodes.summary: Enterprise digital-asset infrastructure company spanning payments, custody, prime brokerage, treasury and stablecoin products while supporting XRPL ecosystem development.
nodes.boundary: Ripple does not own XRPL, issue every XRPL asset or become a transfer agent through a technology relationship.

nodes.label: Ripple National Trust Bank
nodes.summary: Proposed Ripple subsidiary with preliminary OCC approval for fiduciary digital-asset custody and planned RLUSD reserve-management functions.
nodes.boundary: Not an operating bank, current RLUSD issuer, Reserve Bank account holder or source of proved production volume.

nodes.label: BlackRock
nodes.summary: Led Securitize's 2024 strategic round, obtained a named Securitize board seat and sponsors BUIDL.
nodes.boundary: Investment and board influence do not establish that BlackRock controls every Securitize entity or Wormhole.

nodes.label: Hamilton Lane
nodes.summary: Participated in Securitize's strategic financing and uses the platform for tokenized products.
nodes.boundary: Investor and client roles are distinct from parent control.

nodes.label: Tradeweb Markets
nodes.summary: Participated in Securitize's strategic financing and was listed among investors rolling interests into the public-company transaction.
nodes.boundary: No reviewed source establishes operating control over Securitize's regulated subsidiaries.

nodes.label: Jump Crypto
nodes.summary: Listed among Securitize investors and describes Wormhole as a protocol arising from Jump's infrastructure-building history.
nodes.boundary: Historical origin and investment adjacency do not prove current control of Wormhole or Securitize.

nodes.label: Securitize Transfer Agent, LLC
nodes.status: SEC-registered transfer agent · current group name
nodes.summary: The named U.S. transfer-agent legal entity in the current Securitize group; older TA and BUIDL documents use Securitize, LLC while current subsidiary and BlackRock product filings use Securitize Transfer Agent, LLC.
nodes.boundary: Its registration does not attach automatically to Securitize Markets, Ripple, Wormhole or every tokenized product.

nodes.label: Securitize Markets, LLC
nodes.summary: Separate broker-dealer and ATS operator supporting placement and secondary trading; the company's SEC-filed Q2 release says FINRA approved tokenized-security custody plus underwriting and selling-group participation.
nodes.boundary: Broker-dealer/ATS permissions are not transfer-agent authority and do not make every token or venue registered.

nodes.label: Securitize Capital, LLC
nodes.summary: The group's investment-adviser entity; its status changed from exempt reporting adviser to full SEC registration in July 2026.
nodes.boundary: Adviser status is a different permission clock from transfer agency, brokerage and fund administration.

nodes.label: Securitize Fund Services, LLC
nodes.summary: Fund-administration arm expanded through the MG Stover acquisition and reported separately from tokenization and brokerage roles.
nodes.boundary: Fund administration is not legal-title authority merely because it includes servicing and recordkeeping functions.

nodes.label: Standard Custody & Trust Company, LLC
nodes.summary: Ripple's acquired New York limited-purpose trust company and the U.S. issuing legal person for RLUSD.
nodes.boundary: Ripple's brand, the trust-company issuer, RLUSD token contracts and reserve custodian are separate control surfaces.

nodes.label: Ripple Prime
nodes.summary: Prime-brokerage and market-access product line built around Ripple's completed Hidden Road acquisition.
nodes.boundary: The product brand is not the exact DTC or FICC member legal entity, and access does not prove XRPL, XRP or RLUSD use.

nodes.label: Ripple Custody
nodes.summary: Institutional custody product and policy layer assembled from Ripple technology and acquired capabilities.
nodes.boundary: The marketed product, acquired companies and customer legal records are separate objects.

nodes.label: Ripple Treasury
nodes.summary: Corporate treasury-management product built on GTreasury and presented with native digital-asset capabilities.
nodes.boundary: A treasury software product does not operate Swift, customer bank accounts or external settlement systems.

nodes.label: ZILO Technology
nodes.summary: Digital recordkeeping and fund-administration technology for asset managers, custodians and transfer agents, including tokenized share classes.
nodes.boundary: Reviewed sources establish technology and a strategic investment, not acquisition or U.S. registered-transfer-agent status.

nodes.label: Licuido
nodes.summary: Tokenization, issuance, distribution and collateral-mobility platform positioned for XRPL-based market use.
nodes.boundary: A company announcement does not prove completed scale, universal liquidity or title authority.

nodes.label: Evernorth Holdings Inc.
nodes.status: public company · business combination completed Oct 9, 2026
nodes.summary: Separate XRP treasury company. Its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II was completed on October 9, 2026, and its XRPN shares were expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on October 12, 2026. At closing it reported holding about 473 million XRP.
nodes.boundary: Ripple is a named investor, not Evernorth's proven parent; the closing release does not say whether Ripple's investment closed.

nodes.label: Pathfinder Digital Assets LLC
nodes.status: Ripple sole member before proposed close
nodes.summary: Pre-combination operating company through which Ripple's controlled XRP-treasury interest enters the proposed Evernorth structure.
nodes.boundary: Pre-close Ripple control of Pathfinder does not make Evernorth a Ripple subsidiary or prove that Pathfinder inventory funds Ripple Payments routes.

nodes.label: BitGo Bank & Trust, National Association
nodes.summary: Custody and escrow provider identified for the XRP reported by Evernorth and Pathfinder before the proposed business-combination close.
nodes.boundary: Custody does not transfer beneficial ownership, permit unrestricted pledge or establish that the assets support a tokenized security, payment route or live lending protocol.

nodes.label: XRPL Single Asset Vault (XLS-65)
nodes.summary: Proposed XRPL primitive designed to pool one asset from depositors for use by on-ledger protocols.
nodes.boundary: A proposal, devnet implementation or mainnet vote does not establish activation, deposits, custody finality, production volume or stress performance.

nodes.label: XRPL Lending Protocol (XLS-66)
nodes.summary: Proposed fixed-term, fixed-rate on-ledger lending protocol using Single Asset Vault liquidity and off-ledger underwriting and risk management.
nodes.boundary: The documented loans are uncollateralized. Protocol automation does not supply underwriting authority, legal perfection, a public backstop or proven production use.

nodes.label: Fubon Bank (Hong Kong) Limited
nodes.summary: Bank participant that used tokenized property-lien claims as collateral in the HKMA e-HKD Phase 1 home-equity lending pilot with Ripple.
nodes.boundary: The pilot used hypothetical e-HKD and does not establish a current production mortgage, digital-title or XRPL collateral service.

nodes.label: Fubon–Ripple property-lien collateral pilot
nodes.summary: A bounded model in which property-lien tokens were loaded into a vault as collateral and hypothetical e-HKD loan proceeds were disbursed under bank instruction.
nodes.boundary: The tokens represented bank charges rather than title deeds; the event was a pilot and supplied no production, scale or stress evidence.

nodes.label: BlackRock BUIDL
nodes.status: live tokenized fund · seven named chains
nodes.summary: BlackRock's tokenized liquidity-fund shares, serviced through Securitize with named share classes on Ethereum, Solana, Avalanche, Aptos, Arbitrum, Optimism and Polygon and enabled for multichain movement and RLUSD exchange functionality.
nodes.boundary: The fund share, transfer-agent record, chain representation and RLUSD received on exchange remain separate claims.

nodes.label: VanEck VBILL
nodes.summary: VanEck tokenized Treasury-fund shares supported by Securitize and an RLUSD smart-contract exchange path.
nodes.boundary: Availability of an exchange path does not make RLUSD the fund's share register or make XRP required.

nodes.label: Ripple USD (RLUSD)
nodes.summary: Dollar stablecoin used as a cash and settlement leg in Ripple's institutional stack and as an exchange option for selected tokenized fund shares.
nodes.boundary: RLUSD success is not XRP success; issuance, reserves, custody, token contracts and distribution are distinct.

nodes.label: XRP
nodes.summary: Native XRPL asset that can participate in path payments and bridge conversion when a route actually selects it.
nodes.boundary: No reviewed relationship, acquisition or gross network volume proves recurring institutional XRP intermediation or persistent financed XRP inventory.

nodes.label: XRP Ledger (XRPL)
nodes.summary: Public ledger supporting issued assets, native XRP, decentralized exchange functions and institution-facing tokenization infrastructure.
nodes.boundary: Ripple is a major builder and ecosystem participant, not the sole legal owner or operator of the public network.

nodes.label: Wormhole interoperability protocol
nodes.summary: Cross-chain messaging and token-transfer infrastructure selected by Securitize and integrated with XRPL/XRPL EVM; RLUSD multichain support uses Wormhole standards.
nodes.boundary: Wormhole transports messages or supported representations. It is not the issuer, transfer agent, custodian, regulator or legal-title authority.

nodes.label: Linked electronic systems and DLT components
nodes.status: proposal permits one or more components
nodes.summary: Databases, blockchains and distributed ledgers may operate as components of the master securityholder file when kept inside the recordkeeping transfer agent's control environment.
nodes.boundary: Technical linkage does not make every component co-authoritative or transfer the agent's legal accountability.

nodes.label: Wallet and on-chain position records
nodes.summary: Wallet addresses and on-chain balances may supply position detail within a controlled electronic record architecture.
nodes.boundary: Possession of a private key or token balance is not automatically conclusive legal title under the proposal.

nodes.label: Ethereum / ETH
nodes.summary: EVM execution layer on which ETH pays transaction gas, validators receive priority fees and protocol issuance, and the base fee is burned; BUIDL has a named Ethereum share class.
nodes.boundary: Ethereum execution and ETH economics do not determine the authoritative holder record or legal rights in a tokenized security.

nodes.label: Solana / SOL
nodes.summary: Solana is a public network that executes and records token transactions. SOL pays network fees. A stablecoin or fund share on Solana remains its issuer’s claim; reserves, the legally authoritative holder record and cash redemption belong to named institutions.
nodes.boundary: Fee payment and token execution do not make Solana the issuer, transfer agent or legal register.

nodes.label: Avalanche / AVAX
nodes.status: BUIDL network · AVAX Primary Network fees
nodes.summary: Avalanche Primary Network execution uses AVAX for fees and burns transaction fees; BUIDL has a named Avalanche share class.
nodes.boundary: Independent Avalanche L1s can have different fee designs, and no chain deployment displaces the transfer agent's authoritative record by itself.

nodes.label: Arbitrum One
nodes.summary: Ethereum rollup where users pay fees in ETH for L2 execution plus the cost of posting data to Ethereum; BUIDL has a named Arbitrum share class.
nodes.boundary: ARB governance and ETH fee mechanics are separate, and rollup settlement does not determine tokenized-security title.

nodes.label: OP Mainnet
nodes.summary: OP Stack rollup where transaction fees are paid in ETH and combine execution, L1 data and operator components; BUIDL has a named Optimism share class.
nodes.boundary: OP governance and ETH fee mechanics are separate, and the rollup does not become a transfer agent or title authority.

nodes.label: Polygon PoS / POL
nodes.summary: EVM-compatible PoS network where POL is used for gas and staking; BUIDL has a named Polygon share class.
nodes.boundary: POL utility and validator economics do not establish the legal ownership record for a represented fund share.

nodes.label: Aptos / APT
nodes.summary: Move-based execution network where transaction gas is charged in APT; BUIDL has a named Aptos share class.
nodes.boundary: APT fee demand and ledger execution do not make Aptos the issuer, transfer agent or legal-title authority.

nodes.label: The Bank of New York Mellon
nodes.summary: Named primary custodian for RLUSD reserves, separate from the issuing trust company and token administrator.
nodes.boundary: Reserve custody does not make BNY the token issuer or transfer agent for tokenized securities. Public sources do not establish BNY operation of XRPL, use of XRP or issuance of tokenized deposits on XRPL.

nodes.label: Custodians, brokers, ATSs, exchanges and fund administrators
nodes.summary: The service layer that may custody assets, route orders, operate venues, administer funds or provide technology around the authoritative record chain.
nodes.boundary: These functions remain role-specific; technical or commercial participation does not confer transfer-agent authority.

nodes.label: DTC / FICC access
nodes.summary: Depository and government-securities clearing access held through Hidden Road Partners CIV US LLC, now within Ripple Prime.
nodes.boundary: Membership is attached to the named legal entity; it does not prove DTC/FICC settlement on XRPL or use of XRP/RLUSD.

nodes.label: Swift connectivity
nodes.summary: Bank-messaging connectivity present in GTreasury's corporate treasury environment and therefore adjacent to Ripple Treasury's adapter layer.
nodes.boundary: Ripple does not own or operate Swift, and a software connection is not Swift settlement or endorsement of XRPL.

nodes.label: Ripple SEC policy submission
nodes.summary: Ripple's written input to the SEC Crypto Task Force advocates a framework for on-chain registries and tokenized securities.
nodes.boundary: A regulated party's requested policy position is not Commission adoption, approval or a compliance finding.

nodes.label: Hidden Road Partners CIV US LLC
nodes.summary: The exact reviewed Ripple Prime subsidiary holding named access to DTC and FICC Government Securities Division.
nodes.boundary: Permissions attach to this legal entity, not automatically to Ripple Labs, XRPL, XRP or RLUSD.

nodes.label: Metaco
nodes.summary: Institutional digital-asset custody technology company acquired by Ripple and incorporated into the custody product line.
nodes.boundary: The acquired company and the marketed Ripple Custody product are distinct objects.

nodes.label: Palisade
nodes.summary: Wallet and custody technology acquired to broaden Ripple's institutional custody capabilities.
nodes.boundary: Acquisition does not make Ripple the beneficial owner or legal recordkeeper for customer assets.

nodes.label: GTreasury
nodes.status: acquired in 2025 · exact close date unresolved
nodes.summary: Corporate treasury-management company now presented as the foundation of Ripple Treasury.
nodes.boundary: The reviewed announcement began as an acquisition agreement; later Ripple pages confirm acquisition in 2025 without establishing the exact close date used by the earlier map.

nodes.label: Rail
nodes.summary: Stablecoin payments infrastructure associated with Ripple's broader payments stack.
nodes.boundary: The reviewed source establishes an acquisition agreement and later integrated product positioning; the exact legal close clock remains unresolved here.

nodes.label: Ripple Payments
nodes.summary: Enterprise cross-border payments product using a combination of digital-asset and fiat rails according to route and jurisdiction.
nodes.boundary: Product branding does not prove that every route uses XRP, XRPL or RLUSD.

nodes.label: Ripple Custody Wallet-as-a-Service
nodes.summary: Institutional wallet infrastructure delivered through Ripple's custody product suite.
nodes.boundary: Wallet technology does not itself determine legal title, transfer-agent records or final settlement.

nodes.label: XRPL DEX and pathfinding
nodes.summary: Ledger-native order books, liquidity paths and payment routing can select available assets for a requested payment outcome.
nodes.boundary: Technical path availability is not proof that XRP is selected or that deep institutional liquidity exists on a given route.

nodes.label: XRPL EVM sidechain
nodes.summary: EVM-compatible execution environment connected to XRPL and included in the reviewed Wormhole integration.
nodes.boundary: A sidechain has distinct execution and bridge assumptions and does not become the XRPL mainnet legal record.

nodes.label: Depository Trust Company
nodes.summary: New York limited-purpose trust company, Federal Reserve member and SEC-registered clearing agency operating the tokenization service.
nodes.boundary: DTC participant status and records remain exact; this is not issuer-register title.

nodes.label: FICC Government Securities Division
nodes.summary: Government-securities clearing utility to which Hidden Road Partners CIV US LLC holds reviewed membership.
nodes.boundary: Membership belongs to the named legal entity and does not establish a crypto settlement path.

nodes.label: Ethereum Foundation
nodes.summary: Supports Ethereum research, development and ecosystem work without owning the public network.
nodes.boundary: Influence and funding are not unilateral protocol control or ownership of applications and assets.

nodes.label: Ethereum open governance process
nodes.status: open proposal and client adoption process
nodes.summary: Protocol change proceeds through public proposals, research, implementation and adoption across the ecosystem.
nodes.boundary: No single company or foundation can by itself bind every user, validator, client or application.

nodes.label: Ethereum execution and consensus clients
nodes.summary: Client teams implement the protocol software used by nodes and validators.
nodes.boundary: A client team does not own the network or the assets executed through it.

nodes.label: Ethereum validators
nodes.summary: Validators stake ETH, propose and attest to blocks, and secure consensus under the protocol rules.
nodes.boundary: Consensus operation does not confer issuer, custodian or transfer-agent authority.

nodes.label: EVM smart contracts
nodes.summary: Deterministic application code executes on Ethereum and can implement tokens, settlement logic and control permissions.
nodes.boundary: Contract execution does not resolve off-chain legal rights or make code the authoritative register by default.

nodes.label: ERC token contracts
nodes.summary: Common interfaces let issuers and applications create fungible and non-fungible token representations.
nodes.boundary: The issuer or application controls the represented asset and its legal terms; Ethereum does not issue every ERC token.

nodes.label: Ether (ETH)
nodes.summary: Native network asset used for fees and proof-of-stake security, with base-fee burn and protocol issuance.
nodes.boundary: Network utility and value capture do not make ETH the backing or legal asset of every Ethereum application.

nodes.label: Ethereum layer-2 systems
nodes.summary: Rollups execute activity above Ethereum and post data or proofs back to the base layer under distinct designs.
nodes.boundary: Each L2 adds its own operators, upgrade keys, bridges and settlement assumptions.

nodes.label: Ethereum issuers and application operators
nodes.summary: Issuers, custodians and application operators control contracts, redemptions and off-chain legal obligations for their own assets.
nodes.boundary: Their authority is not Ethereum protocol ownership and must be evaluated product by product.

nodes.label: Hedera Governing Council
nodes.summary: Council members govern network policy and oversee the public Hedera network under the published governance model.
nodes.boundary: Council governance is distinct from ownership of user applications and tokenized assets.

nodes.label: Hiero open-source project
nodes.summary: Open-source project housing reviewed Hedera-related core code and developer components.
nodes.boundary: Open-source stewardship does not itself determine network policy or application legal rights.

nodes.label: Hedera public mainnet
nodes.summary: Public distributed ledger using hashgraph consensus and native services for tokens, contracts and consensus messaging.
nodes.boundary: Network consensus is not issuer, transfer-agent or custodian authority.

nodes.label: Hedera native services
nodes.status: live token, contract and consensus services
nodes.summary: Network-level services provide tokenization, smart contracts and consensus timestamps.
nodes.boundary: Service availability does not make Hedera the legal issuer or authoritative holder record.

nodes.label: HBAR
nodes.summary: Native asset used for network fees and security economics.
nodes.boundary: HBAR is not the backing or legal instrument represented by enterprise tokens on Hedera.

nodes.label: HashSphere
nodes.summary: Institution-oriented application environment built around Hedera technology and controlled deployment needs.
nodes.boundary: An application environment has its own operators and permissions; it is not identical to the public mainnet.

nodes.label: Archax
nodes.summary: Regulated digital-asset operator using Hedera in the reviewed enterprise case study.
nodes.boundary: Archax retains regulated and issuer-facing duties; Hedera supplies technology rather than the legal permission.

nodes.label: Hedera-issued enterprise assets
nodes.summary: Tokens created with Hedera services under issuer and application controls.
nodes.boundary: Each asset's issuer, terms and off-chain records remain decisive.

nodes.label: Hedera interoperability layer
nodes.summary: Cross-chain connection expanding Hedera's reach to other on-chain environments.
nodes.boundary: Transport does not preserve legal title automatically or become the asset issuer.

nodes.label: Stellar Development Foundation
nodes.summary: Supports Stellar protocol development and ecosystem adoption.
nodes.boundary: Foundation stewardship is not ownership of every validator, anchor, issuer or asset.

nodes.label: Stellar public ledger
nodes.summary: Public ledger supporting payments, issued assets, offers and application functions.
nodes.boundary: Ledger settlement does not make Stellar the issuer or legal recordkeeper for every asset.

nodes.label: Stellar validators
nodes.summary: Validators reach agreement under the Stellar Consensus Protocol using configured trust relationships.
nodes.boundary: Validator participation does not confer asset-issuer or custodial authority.

nodes.label: Soroban smart contracts
nodes.summary: Smart-contract environment extending the Stellar ledger with programmable applications.
nodes.boundary: Application code and operators remain separate from base-ledger governance and legal rights.

nodes.label: Lumens (XLM)
nodes.summary: Native Stellar asset used for network fees and minimum balance requirements.
nodes.boundary: XLM is not the backing or issuer liability for every asset represented on Stellar.

nodes.label: Stellar asset issuers
nodes.summary: Organizations create issued assets and define redemption and authorization terms.
nodes.boundary: Issuer obligations sit outside the Stellar protocol and vary by asset.

nodes.label: Stellar anchors
nodes.summary: Businesses connect fiat, deposits, withdrawals and issued assets to the Stellar network.
nodes.boundary: Anchor claims and customer protections depend on the named entity and jurisdiction.

nodes.label: Franklin OnChain U.S. Government Money Fund / BENJI
nodes.summary: Registered fund with a blockchain-integrated shareholder-record model and a multi-year Stellar deployment.
nodes.boundary: Fund shares, transfer-agent records and on-chain representations remain governed by the fund's legal structure.

nodes.label: MoneyGram Access on Stellar
nodes.summary: Cash-in and cash-out access linking users and supported Stellar assets through MoneyGram services.
nodes.boundary: The access provider controls its own customer, compliance and cash obligations.

nodes.label: DTC Stellar tokenization connection
nodes.summary: DTC announced work to connect its tokenization service with the Stellar public blockchain.
nodes.boundary: An announced connection is not completed production, universal asset support or delegation of DTC's legal records.

nodes.label: Digital Asset

nodes.label: Canton Foundation

nodes.label: Canton Global Synchronizer

nodes.label: Canton super validators
nodes.summary: Operators performing shared-network governance and validation functions around the Global Synchronizer.

nodes.label: Canton participant validators

nodes.boundary: Each participant controls its domain and obligations rather than sharing all data with the network.

nodes.label: Canton Coin

nodes.label: Canton synchronized applications

nodes.label: DTC Canton tokenization connection
nodes.summary: DTC's tokenization service identifies Canton among reviewed connection environments.
nodes.boundary: Connection does not make Canton DTC's authoritative record or establish universal production use.

nodes.label: Solana Foundation

nodes.label: Solana validators

nodes.boundary: Validation does not confer issuer, custodian or legal-record authority.

nodes.label: Solana programs and account runtime

nodes.label: Solana Token-2022 program

nodes.label: SOL

nodes.label: Solana token issuers

nodes.label: Solana Attestation Service

nodes.label: Avalanche Primary Network validators

nodes.label: AVAX

nodes.label: Custom Avalanche L1s

nodes.label: Avalanche Evergreen

nodes.label: Chainlink Labs

nodes.label: Chainlink decentralized oracle networks

nodes.label: LINK
nodes.summary: Token used in Chainlink service economics and staking mechanisms.

nodes.label: Chainlink Data Feeds

nodes.label: Chainlink CCIP

nodes.label: Chainlink Runtime Environment

nodes.label: Chainlink Payment Abstraction

nodes.label: Chainlink financial-market infrastructure integrations

nodes.label: Bitcoin Core
nodes.summary: Open-source software project maintaining a widely used Bitcoin node implementation.

nodes.label: Bitcoin full nodes
nodes.summary: Nodes independently validate blocks and transactions against the rules they run.
nodes.boundary: Node validation does not create a legal claim against custodians or payment providers.

nodes.label: Bitcoin miners
nodes.summary: Miners assemble candidate blocks and perform proof of work to order valid transactions.
nodes.boundary: Miners cannot by themselves make invalid transactions valid or determine off-chain ownership.

nodes.label: Bitcoin base network
nodes.summary: Public transaction and settlement network validated by nodes and extended through proof of work.
nodes.boundary: Base-chain finality is distinct from intermediary account records and legal remedies.

nodes.label: Bitcoin (BTC)
nodes.summary: Native scarce asset transferred on the Bitcoin network.
nodes.boundary: A custodial BTC claim, fund share and on-chain UTXO are different legal and operational objects.

nodes.label: Bitcoin transaction fee market
nodes.summary: Users attach fees and miners select transactions for limited block space.
nodes.boundary: Fee demand secures inclusion economics but does not prove broader token-value capture or legal settlement.

nodes.label: Lightning Network

nodes.label: Bitcoin custodians, exchanges and ETP records

edges.label: proposes one accountable recordkeeper
edges.claim: One registered recordkeeping transfer agent would remain responsible for and in exclusive control of the master securityholder file for a fungible issue, even across linked systems and service companies.
edges.boundary: Not final; the release asks about alternatives.

edges.label: preserves issuer and governing-law starting point
edges.claim: The proposal modernizes transfer-agent records without replacing the issuer and governing corporate law as the source of the security and recognized holder rights.
edges.boundary: This is an architectural reading of the proposal, not a new federal charter for tokenized securities.

edges.label: appoints accountable recordkeeper for the issue
edges.claim: The issuer's security issue is maintained through a registered recordkeeping transfer agent under the proposed one-agent accountability model.
edges.boundary: The proposal asks whether alternative shared-responsibility arrangements should be permitted.

edges.label: responsible for and in exclusive control
edges.claim: The recordkeeping transfer agent would be responsible for and in exclusive control of the authoritative master securityholder file.
edges.boundary: Exclusive control is proposed, not yet an effective final-rule requirement.

edges.label: may comprise linked electronic components
edges.claim: One or more linked databases, blockchains or distributed ledgers may be components of the master securityholder file.
edges.boundary: Component status does not make every ledger separately authoritative.

edges.label: may include wallet-position detail
edges.claim: Wallet addresses and on-chain position data may be recorded inside the controlled electronic file architecture.
edges.boundary: Wallet control and legal ownership can diverge.

edges.label: owns procedures and outsourced dependencies
edges.claim: Written procedures, annual governing-body approval and service-provider oversight would keep outsourced technology inside the regulated control environment.
edges.boundary: Outsourcing does not outsource legal accountability.

edges.label: reports tokenization operating model
edges.claim: Registered transfer agents would report issuer-sponsored versus third-party tokenization, DLT use, security type and service providers.
edges.boundary: Reported use is not SEC approval.

edges.label: controls legends, errors and corrections
edges.claim: The proposal would add restrictive-legend controls and asks how correction or deletion duties should work with immutable records.
edges.boundary: The Commission has not finalized an immutable-ledger correction method.

edges.label: interfaces with downstream service layer
edges.claim: The controlled record system may interface with custodians, brokers, ATSs, exchanges, fund administrators and other service providers.
edges.boundary: Interfacing does not merge their permissions or make them co-recordkeepers.

edges.label: named entity is registered TA
edges.claim: The transfer-agent entity historically filed as Securitize, LLC and currently disclosed as Securitize Transfer Agent, LLC is a registered transfer agent and is the closest named entity in this map to the proposed recordkeeping role.

sources.label: CFTC swap-data reporting rules

sources.label: CFTC swap data repository rules
sources.boundary: Part 49 governs a CFTC swap data repository's statutory duties. It does not make a reporting counterparty, technical delegate, or ledger operator an SDR.

sources.label: CFTC industry filings: Swap Data Repositories
sources.boundary: The listed status, asset class, and entity name control. It does not prove a participant agreement, a reportable transaction, or current acceptance of a particular record.

sources.label: CFTC final Part 45 rulemaking: third-party reporting facilitation
sources.boundary: A reporting counterparty may use a third-party facilitator, but that contractual delegation does not move the underlying reporting responsibility or turn the facilitator into an SDR.

sources.label: SEC Regulation SBSR reporting and dissemination framework
sources.boundary: Applies to security-based swaps under the SEC framework, which is separate from the CFTC swap regime and from ordinary securities-token recordkeeping.

sources.label: SEC approval of DTCC Data Repository (U.S), LLC as security-based swap data repository
sources.boundary: This is an SEC security-based-swap repository authorization for the stated asset classes, not an authorization for the CFTC SDR entity bearing a similar name or for tokenized securities generally.

Mastercard, BVNK and other partners can provide wallets, conversion, sending, receiving or settlement interfaces without inheriting Bridge's issuer obligation.
An eligible redemption request returns to Bridge for compliance review and token burn under the issuer terms.
Bank USD payout, legal discharge, correction and loss allocation remain separate endpoints; no public launch-day Mastercard customer receipt or cross-party failure waterfall closes them.

mapping_steps.boundary: Partner access is mapped, but provider-specific contracts, eligibility, fees and production state differ.
Reserve classes and named institutions are public; exact mandates, account title, cash receipt and priority are not.
Issuer, supply and aggregate reconciliation are mapped; transaction-level incoming cash and liability posting are not.
Four native deployments and launch supply are mapped; a common cross-chain finality and recovery mechanism is not.
Advertised and named routes are mapped; no named Mastercard production customer or route volume is public.
Issuer terms establish the obligation and controls; no launch-day stress redemption or transaction-specific burn receipt is mapped.
Cash posting, legal discharge and the cross-party failure waterfall remain unresolved endpoints.

asset_traces.mapping_note: Launch-day architecture. The trace deliberately preserves issuer, governance, reserve, distributor, chain, redemption, bank-payout and remedy clocks rather than presenting a single atomic payment.

accounting_layers.label: 1 · Who owes whom?
accounting_layers.explanation: A customer deposit is the customer’s asset and the bank’s liability. A token representation does not automatically create a second independent claim.
accounting_layers.question: Who is the issuer or debtor, and what exact right does the holder own?

accounting_layers.label: 2 · Custody & access
accounting_layers.explanation: Deposits, segregated custody and control of keys are different arrangements. Identify the asset holder, account provider and person authorized to move value.
accounting_layers.question: Where is the value held, who controls it and who is allowed to instruct?

accounting_layers.label: 3 · Funding & inventory
accounting_layers.explanation: Funding confirmed before execution does not mean final settlement has occurred. Reservation, credit, collateral and prefunding carry different exposures.
accounting_layers.question: What balance, credit or collateral supports the payment, for how long and at whose cost?

accounting_layers.label: 4 · Shared commitment
accounting_layers.explanation: A shared record lets relevant parties coordinate payment state. An informational record is not automatically a separate financial asset or the authoritative legal register.
accounting_layers.question: What is authorized, recorded and executed; who can see it; what makes the commitment binding?

accounting_layers.label: 5 · Clearing & netting
accounting_layers.explanation: Matching agrees the obligations; netting calculates an offset amount under applicable rules. Neither alone supplies a settlement asset or guarantee.
accounting_layers.question: Are obligations matched, netted, novated or guaranteed—and by whom?

accounting_layers.label: 6 · Cash & finality
accounting_layers.explanation: Customer credit, technical confirmation, cash settlement and legal finality can occur at different times. Identify which books discharge the obligation.
accounting_layers.question: What asset settles the payment, which record controls and when is discharge final?

accounting_layers.label: 7 · Failure & remedy
accounting_layers.explanation: If the recipient can spend before banks settle and settlement fails, a contract and a balance sheet must carry the gap.
accounting_layers.question: Who can correct or reverse, who bears loss, and what stress evidence exists?

evidence_questions.label: Who finances the interval?
evidence_questions.finding: Banks validated funding and managed the interval before external settlement. Customer availability can precede bank cash receipt.
evidence_questions.unknown: Prefunded account, reservation, credit facility, collateral, amount and duration are not disclosed for Siemens.
evidence_questions.needed: Funding account and control, release conditions, credit/security agreement and stage timestamps.
evidence_questions.comparison: Compare the funding mechanism and when money becomes usable. Earlier availability alone does not prove unsecured lending.

evidence_questions.label: When is the commitment binding—and who bears failure?
evidence_questions.finding: SWIFT confirms interbank obligations; banks settle through external rails. Public descriptions refer to defined rules.
evidence_questions.unknown: Binding event, record priority, cancellation cutoff, customer-credit irrevocability and default loss allocation are not publicly established.
evidence_questions.needed: Versioned participant terms, authoritative-record hierarchy, finality and cancellation/default schedules.
evidence_questions.comparison: Software confirmation, a binding debt and legal discharge are separate states. An unfilled legal-finality cell remains an evidence gap.

evidence_questions.label: Who carries the FX exposure?
evidence_questions.finding: The banks validated FX arrangements for Siemens’ EUR account in France to GBP account in the UK.
evidence_questions.unknown: Dealer, quote-lock time, hedge, value date and payment-versus-payment protection are not disclosed.
evidence_questions.needed: FX confirmation and each currency leg’s irrevocability, finality and replacement/unwind terms.
evidence_questions.comparison: Separate price/replacement risk, principal settlement risk and liquidity delay. Account location does not identify the FX dealer.

evidence_questions.label: Can this liquidity be reused on another network?
evidence_questions.finding: Selected bank routes show transfer, conversion or redemption. Agorá tests used earmarking/designated accounts, locks and later external redemption.
evidence_questions.unknown: One freely spendable balance across SWIFT, Partior, Kinexys, Canton and Agorá—and quantified shared cash savings—are not established.
evidence_questions.needed: Issuer and account identity, transfer/redemption route, encumbrance, operating hours and before/after funding requirements.
evidence_questions.comparison: Common bank participation is an entity overlap. A demonstrated transfer is a route overlap. Neither alone establishes a shared balance.

liquidity_hub.title: Liquidity
